Thus, the focus shifts from interpersonal relationships to the physicality of things, simultaneously formulating a distance from the anthropocentric perspective. The characteristic thick, massive color application remains central. Layer upon layer, Krauss applies oil paint to the canvas and creates relief-like surfaces that resemble geological sediments. Like natural layers, they store time, movement, and material. The new work series begins with observations of urban spaces. Architecture appears as a sedimentary store of cultural and material processes; limestone, clay, or bricks become references to a materiality that is equally built like organically grown. Through the fluctuating biographies of nine artists and their works – including paintings, sculptures, ceramics, and photographs – it shows how differently the artists navigated the political and social conditions of their time. To what extent did sexual orientation influence their artistic practice and professional development? Homosexuality remained in the GDR, despite gradual decriminalization, strongly stigmatized socially and politically. After the fall of the Berlin Wall, the situation for queer artists did not significantly improve – rather, many artists from the GDR were at risk of being forgotten. Today, there is growing general interest in the art and culture of the GDR as well as in queer life realities. Richard Oelze passed away in 1980 at the age of 80, having retreated to Posteholz in the Weserbergland. However, his paintings still captivate us to this day. Since the 1970s, Gallery Brockstedt has worked intensively with him and now presents a museum exhibition of his oil paintings and drawings. The painter born in 1900 is considered one of the most independent German artists of the 20th century. His enigmatic image worlds move between Surrealism, New Objectivity, and a deeply personal form of reality observation. In atmospherically condensed landscapes and mysterious figure constellations, scenes emerge that appear familiar and simultaneously resist any unique interpretation. After his training at the Bauhaus in Weimar and Dessau, Oelze came to Paris in the 1930s with the international Surrealism - the artist group around André Breton. He also learned there to know established artists like Salvador Dalí and Max Ernst, who was one of the greatest admirers of Oelze's work. Ernst valued Oelze's highly detailed, dreamlike paintings very much and allegedly considered them 'the best dream painting.' In terms of artistic techniques, there were strong parallels: Max Ernst's development of decalcomania (a stamping process in which random, organic structures emerge through pressed color) strongly influenced Oelze. He used similar principles to bring psychological phenomena such as pareidolia (recognizing faces and shapes in abstract structures) to perfection on the canvas. […]

Salim Green describes his interdisciplinary practice as a process in which 'things are defined by their contours.' In his work, he frequently draws on speculative models such as the 'Dark Forest Theory' and related concepts to process lived experiences. With their persistent focus on the unrecognizability and interiority, Green's works resist the magnetism of fixed meanings or clearly defined identifications and rely on strategies of concealment, opacity, and illegibility, which stem from the experience of Black people. The title 'Sugarshack' refers to an expression used by the artist's father to describe abandoned or decaying buildings in his hometown of Waterloo, Iowa. As a significant production and industrial center in the Midwest, Waterloo became a destination for African Americans during the 'Great Migration,' who left the racially segregated South; many were recruited by the railroad to break strikes. For the newcomers, freight cars were provided as temporary housing alongside the tracks in the eastern part of the city before they built their homes in the same area - the only part of the city that was open to them at the time due to restrictive housing regulations in Waterloo - many of which have since left.
